title: The dark night
hook: John of the Cross wrote of a dark night where prayer feels empty and something deeper grows

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa's interior castle. Your line was many rooms. Did a doorway catch you, and did you take one breath a room further in? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

For years, morning prayer was the best part of her day. Warm. Easy. Words came. Today, nothing. Not anger, not doubt exactly. Just flat, like chewing paper. Tomorrow, the same. And the next week. She starts to wonder what she's done wrong. Teresa's friend and fellow Carmelite, a friar called John of the Cross, wrote a poem about a night like that, and then wrote a whole book explaining the poem. His surprising claim is that the flatness might not mean something has gone wrong at all. Today's word is his name for it.
screen: `IT USED TO BE EASY.` → `TODAY, NOTHING.` → `MAYBE NOTHING'S GONE WRONG.`

segments.voice: John's poem begins on a dark night, with someone slipping out of a quiet house, unseen, to meet the one they love. The night isn't the enemy in the poem. Later in it, the night is the guide. Then John wrote a prose book, The Dark Night, to explain what that means for prayer. Here it is, four ways. First, the sweetness goes. John says that beginners often find prayer full of comfort, and then, for a time, God takes the comfort away. The old ways of praying, with pictures and thoughts, stop working. Yesterday's rooms and the day before's gospel scenes may simply go dark. Second, it isn't the same as every dark mood. John was careful here. He gives signs to tell this night apart from ordinary sadness or what he calls melancholy. One sign: the person finds no pleasure in God's things, but no pleasure in other things either. Another: they still care, painfully, about whether they're serving God. A third: they can't meditate with the imagination the way they used to. Third, what to do. John's advice is gentle. Don't strain to force the old feelings back. Rest in peace and quiet, with a simple loving attention, even if it seems like you're wasting time. Fourth, what grows. In John's reading, the night strips away a love that depended on good feelings, so that something quieter and deeper can grow underneath. Some readers today use the phrase dark night of the soul for any hard time. John's own night is narrower, and he took care to say that not every darkness is this one. Hard seasons that weigh on everything deserve a friend, and sometimes a doctor, as well as a prayer.
screen: `THE NIGHT IS THE GUIDE.` · `THE SWEETNESS GOES.` · `NOT EVERY DARK MOOD.` · `REST IN LOVING ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a dry season. Sit still and let your breathing slow. Think of a time when something you loved went flat: a prayer, a friendship, a craft, a job. Don't try to fix it now, and don't try to feel anything special. Just sit beside it, the way you'd sit with a friend who doesn't need advice. If you pray, you can offer the dryness itself, without words. If not, just keep it company. The bell holds the time.
The dark night. In John of the Cross, a season when prayer goes flat and the old comforts fall away, and something quieter grows underneath. Today's word.

Your line: a dark night. Today, if something you usually enjoy feels flat, do it anyway, gently, without forcing the feeling, and see what's still there underneath. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Christians who meet dryness in prayer often talk it over with a spiritual director, who may draw on John of the Cross to help tell a dark night apart from depression or ordinary discouragement.

notes: All John of the Cross material is paraphrased (no translation on the validator's public-domain list). Confirm: the poem's night as guide; God withdrawing consolation from beginners (Book I, ch. 8); the three signs and the distinction from melancholy (I.9); the advice to rest in peace and quiet with loving attention and not strain at meditation (I.10).
The hook's woman is an illustration, not from the text. 'Teresa's friend and fellow Carmelite' is biographical; confirm wording. No dates or prison story included.
The teach adds a gentle line that hard seasons may need a friend or a doctor. Confirm the tone is right and does not overstate John's own distinction.
